utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, Madam, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you speak nearer to the microphone. Your voice is not reaching the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have about ten more minutes of questions for you. If you remember well, yesterday we left off or we concluded as we were discussing the moment when you left the hospital, went into the yard of the hospital as you were preparing for the evacuation. Therefore, I would like to continue with that topic. I would rather not put a photograph in front of you because I think that all of us already have a good picture in our minds of what the hospital yard looked like, but I will just ask you this. As you were then expecting to head towards the buses and evacuation, were you standing in an area which was between the emergency ward building and the hospital entrance? Was that the area where you stood at that time? Would you please give an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present and do you remember when a convoy of medical vehicles arrived in front of the hospital building? Those vehicles were supposed to transport the wounded in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that because I realised that I'd forgotten some of my belongings. And at one point in time I went back to my room so there were certain things that I missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see later on these medical vehicles that had entered the hospital compound, the hospital yard, once you came back? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the wounded were boarded on to those vehicles and who boarded them? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that area, in the yard, awaiting the evacuation, were there women, children, and the elderly with you there as well?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were mostly hospital staff members and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, were you present and did you hear when they were told that they had a choice between going to Serbia, going to Croatia, or remaining in Vukovar? They were told this while standing there in the yard.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was said before, not at that moment, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring strictly to the period when you stood in the yard. Therefore, while you were there in the yard, do you remember seeing at any point in time my client, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Several days ago when testifying in examination-in-chief you explained to my learned friend from the Prosecution that in those hours, as you were waiting and once you reached the bus, you saw for the first time a person you identified as a member of a paramilitary unit. And you said that one could clearly distinguish between them and a member of the regular army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that prior to that, from the morning until that period of time, you did not see them in the hospital yard until that moment when you were waiting for the evacuation to begin?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody with such insignia, not in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of what time it was when you saw those people there.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, as I said, this was around 10.00 when we reached that area, then it must have been between 10.00 and 12.00. I think that would be a correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to go into private session for just one question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either during your testimony here or perhaps in your statement, I can't remember where - and if you do remember then please correct me - you said that you saw three buses waiting for you and about ten ambulances.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite accurate when discussing this. These three buses were not parked within the hospital compound, but rather beyond. They stood in front of the court building. Further, to be fully accurate, the other vehicles, ambulances, I saw them once they joined our convoy. I just wanted to be fully accurate regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained that. You said that you went first to the court building, that you boarded the buses, and then the convoy set out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour those buses were, what licence plates they had? Were those civilian or military buses? Do you remember anything regarding this?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were civilian buses, but I might be wrong. I didn't really look for any of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on your testimony, there were about 54 patients there and 70 to 80 family members in that convoy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the number of patients later on. This is an estimate that I gave you. Later on this figure was confirmed. Now, as to whether it was fully accurate or not, I can't say. As for the family members, that was based on the assessment of how many people could be seated in a bus. It could be ten or 20 people more, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're asked to pause for a moment. There's a -- some form of technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a problem with the voice distortion mechanism; technicians are looking at it. Mr. Lukic, to enable us to continue, we will go into private session. In that way, the technical problem is avoided. It's hoped that the matter can be remedied in about ten minutes, by which time you'll be well finished on your prediction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, during your cross-examination you mentioned that no one physically cut off the water or electricity supply to the hospital. So my question to you is: How were these installations cut off? How did they come to be non-working?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I know and based on my personal conviction, this was caused by the destruction of the installations supplying water and electricity to the hospital, and also within the hospital. The installations, the equipment, was destroyed, therefore continuous supply was impossible. So the destruction occurred both outside the hospital and within the hospital. I have to say, though, that I am no expert, but it is my opinion that this was caused by destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was shelling the hospital?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'd now look to move to another area, Witness, and this concerns the question of the markings of the hospital with the Red Cross insignia which you mentioned in your evidence in chief and in cross-examination. Now, in which month was the markings put on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already said this. I believe it was in September. The marking was placed in the visible, outside area, but I may not be fully accurate about the time period. It could have been August or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how long did the marking remain there?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mention in your evidence in chief that it was Dr. Bosanac who was negotiating with the JNA. So would it have been Dr. Bosanac, if anyone, who would have raised the bombing of the hotel -- sorry, the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question did not arise from any question put during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the question of the distance and whether the visibility and the markings of the Red Cross sign did actually come during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It did. What I'm not immediately grasping is the particular question you're asking and how it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: It arises in connection with whether the party which was bombarding the hospital would have had knowledge from any source that indeed there was a Red Cross marking and that the hospital was being bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you seeking to have the witness indicate whether anybody other than Dr. Bosanac in her knowledge might have been negotiating about the hospital with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, anybody at all, whether Dr. Bosanac or any other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that sufficiently arises, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Agha, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So just coming back to that question, Witness, you had mentioned that Dr. Bosanac was negotiating with the JNA. So is it likely that over this three months' period of bombardment she would have mentioned this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can answer that, Mr. Agha. She knows or she doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dr. Bosanac would have mentioned this to the JNA or any other person she was negotiating with whilst the bombardment was going on?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not based on direct participation and conversations or negotiations. As she not only was supposed to but had to make such a warning, and I don't think that's contentious at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move away from the Red Cross markings and come to the Red Cross themselves. Now, it is your evidence they were expected for the evacuation but they did not arrive. Did you learn why they were delayed or they did not arrive for the evacuation later on?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that they were prevented from arriving in the hospital. That was the information we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was preventing them?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what we learned, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to move to another topic, and this concerns the stream of people, I believe the Defence counsel call it, who gathered at the hospital on 17th of November. Now, can you describe the condition in which these people were in when they were arriving at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrified, first of all. They looked more than miserable. They looked like a person you pulled out from a basement, a person that hasn't had a bath in months, all dusty and dirty. But what was common to all of them was that they were afraid and terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: As a doctor, how humanitarian would it have been for you to send all these people away?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody knocked on your door, you, as a physician or just as a regular person, would never turn them away if they needed help. A doctor, especially, would never do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, just before my learned friend Mr. Lukic finished his cross-examination, he mentioned that when you were escorted or evacuated from hospital, there were 17 doctors and six nurses, roughly, on that convoy and that these figures came from monitors. Now, to your knowledge did most or all of this convoy reach its destination safely?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise information, therefore I cannot claim this with certainty. But I think that except for some minor problems en route, everybody arrived at their destination. Perhaps you can find somewhere more reliable information than what I can provide to you, but I think that everybody who was with me on my bus, all of us arrived safely in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, on the other hand when your patients were -- who were under your care were removed from the hospital by the JNA, how many doctors and nurses were accompanying those patients?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: How many monitors and Red Cross personnel were accompanying your patients?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my information is correct, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how many of your patients who were taken away reached their destination safely, presumably to a hospital for treatment?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be certain about two only.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what about the others?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I marked on that document, the rest of them were killed and are still listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to a final topic, if I may, and that is actually your list which you tendered in evidence of your patients. Now, during cross-examination various questions for put to you as to what the composition of these patients were, whether they were injured, their make-up, et cetera. Now, I just want to clarify that on your list at number 20 is a gentleman named -- if my pronunciation is correct, you'll have to bear with me, Dragutin Friscic who was an uninjured person who you placed on your list. Now what was his status? Was he a fighter, was he a civilian, was he a hospital worker? What was his status?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he was a civilian but please don't hold me to it. There is something that I would like to clarify, if I may. Mr. Lukic asked me about how I knew and how I made the markings. I hope I do have the Chamber's permission to go ahead with this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one particular aspect regarding this. When I talked to the investigators, I had a copy of this list, but then they asked me whether I remembered who was what or what the person's status was. And I notice there's a difference between the list that you have here and my copy that I had at the time based on which I conducted the interview. And back then it was based on my memory that I added details from personal case histories. This is by way of clarification. I'm just wondering why this information does not seem to appear on your list, whereas it is certain that I in fact provided such information to the investigators at the time. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I think it was your questioning, not Mr. Lukic's.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apology. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not about me being vain or anything. I'm not just trying to appear on the transcript. There is something else I wanted to bring up. This additional explanation provided by the witness during my learned friend's re-direct, or before he has actually concluded it, I believe the witness perhaps may need to be examined on these additional circumstances. This is new information and we weren't given the same document. So we would like to know whether she in fact gave this document to the OTP when she was interviewed by the investigators, or perhaps my learned friend could examine the witness on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, taking your points in order, first the witness specifically sought to give this explanation. You specifically told her that she should not at that point and she could be re-examined on it and that is what is now occurring. So you have rather burnt your bridges about an opportunity to question further on that topic. With respect to the list, no doubt Mr. Agha will now be exploring whether there is yet a further copy of the list or one to which some further information was added by the witness at some time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So coming back to the individual in particular, this is Mr. Dragutin Friscic, who you believed was a civilian, is he alive? What is he?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No, he is not alive?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not according to my information, he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, there's another couple of points I need to just clarify from you with regard to your list. Now, during the cross-examination the Defence suggested that up to 14 of your patients may have been former ZNG fighters or MUP. Now, even if this was so, what kind of resistance were these alleged former ZNG fighters or MUP putting up at the hospital when the JNA arrived?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what firearms did they have with them?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that they had no firearms at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And according to your earlier evidence, most of these former alleged fighters had genuine injuries?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, during your cross-examination the Defence also suggested that some of these 14 patients of yours were trying to evade arrest because they may have committed crimes. So on that basis, what questions did the JNA ask your patients before they took them away to determine what crimes they had committed?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about those two gentlemen when I was present as they were being led away. There was no question of that sort, no indication of anything like that. It was only about the wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So what explanation did the JNA give you for taking your patients away?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No explanation was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: When did they tell you that your patients were under arrest?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was said about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: What crimes did they tell you that they were suspected of committing?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As nothing was said about that, nothing was said about them being suspected of committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So where was the trial of your patients heard? Where was that? Was it in a courtroom like this? Did you attend it?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never actually heard that any such trial took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yet your injured, unarmed patients, most of them are alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no further questions in re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, before the witness leaves, we would like to find out what we want to know, not in terms of examination-in-chief, but in terms of our cross-examination but in terms of our relations with the OTP. Something you said and the Prosecutor did not bring up. When she gave the OTP her statement, did she in fact give them the list containing such information as who were members of the ZNG or MUP? Did she give a separate list with those markings? I think we should have that clarified before the witness leaves, and I think you know exactly why that is material to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was about to ask some questions of the witness on this topic because it seems to us to be left in an unsatisfactory state. Now, I propose to do that first and then see what, if anything, I need to raise with Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Madam, if we can go back to the time when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995 and you made a statement. You've mentioned that you had then with you a copy of your patient list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the list you prepared probably on the evening of the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same one that you have. It's the same list, but this one is a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the list you've seen here is the list you prepared on the -- in the hospital in November 1991 and you had with you in 1995 a copy of that list. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was based on that list that I tried to think back and recollect, combined with my knowledge of the patients' case histories, that's what I'm trying to explain, whether somebody was a civilian or a member of the MUP or ZNG. That is why next to each of the names you have these remarks based on the -- what I remembered to be true. I went through that list and what I said I said based on that list. I'm trying to say it's the same list. It's only that it was based on my recollection that I made individual notes next to each of the names. But the list itself was done, as it were, by word of mouth based on that same list I informed the gentleman. That's what I remembered, what I recalled, at the time. It was based on my recollection and on my recollection of patients' case histories. That's what I tried to explain. I'm not sure you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a little more we need to explore. In 1995 in the interview, did you mark additional information on the copy of the list that you had with you?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I understand, then, that reading the names on the list in the interview, you then tried to remember what you could from your knowledge of the case histories in 1991 and things like membership of ZNG or MUP?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did you, from that recollection, tell those you were interviewing what you could remember about membership of ZNG or MUP by the people on the list?

utterances.speaker: P-O21 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the position we seem to have reached is that there is no additional list with different markings, which is what, at one point, seemed to be the position. And I would, from the point of view of the Chamber, be prepared to leave the matter on that basis. Madam, I'm pleased to be able to tell you that that concludes the evidence, the questioning that will occur in this trial of you. The Chamber is grateful for the time you've been here, the assistance you've given, and the effort you've made to come here to assist. You may now go to your home, but if you would stay where you are a moment so that the shutters can be closed before you leave the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, are we ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Thank you very much. May I call Dr. Njavro, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is not -- or he is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The shutters could go up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I ask you to read aloud the affirmation on the card that was given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Juraj Njavro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is correct, is it not, that you are currently a government minister in the Ministry of Health for the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. I am now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, what are your professional qualifications, please?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I completed secondary school, after that the medical school in Zagreb. After that, a residence in general surgery in Belgrade, and then I pursued post-graduate studies specialising in surgery; that was in Zagreb. I worked as a surgeon in the Vukovar Hospital from the very start and during the war of aggression against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it right that you worked for approximately 25 years in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That's right. I worked there from the very beginning just after I finished my residence, the mandatory one. After that I was an assistant in surgery, and after that I pursued specialised studies in general surgery, which I completed at the so-called second surgical clinic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, if I may, please, very briefly from May 1991, to use that as a reference point. Is it right that a number of police officers were killed and injured and brought to the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This occurred on the 2nd of May, 1991, in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Subsequently, is it also right to say that special protocols for treatment of the wounded was put in place at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Prosecutor. It is true that special protocols were established at the hospital and that records were being kept, accurate ones, if I may add, of all the wounded. It was always perfectly clear who was a civilian, who was a member of the MUP, and who was a member of the ZNG, National Guards' Corps. When wounded were brought in, personal information was taken, where they were wounded, how they were wounded, and who brought them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I may just follow that through. In relation to the records themselves, is it correct that they were compiled as best could be on a day-by-day basis up until the removal of patients from the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That is correct. The records were kept in compliance with all the laws that are binding for hospitals, wards and clinics. This was a law that applied throughout the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the records after the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, after the JNA forces and the Chetnik paramilitaries entered the Vukovar Hospital, all these documents, records, both those of the hospital and of the surgery clinic, were taken away, containing information with regard to all those who came to seek help at the Vukovar Hospital, irrespective of whether they were seriously or just slightly wounded. All of this was placed in a bag, and the JNA soldiers took it away from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we very briefly - and I know you've touched on the topic - could we very briefly deal with the procedure for new admissions into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. When someone came to the hospital or was brought there by an ambulance or if there was no need to use ambulance, the person would just simply walk to the hospital, they would report to the surgery clinic, personal information was taken down, first name, last name, year of birth, place of birth, occupation, and who referred them to the hospital. After that, this person would be medically examined, processed, and all their information would be recorded in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In relation to new patients, did the hospital, as far as you are aware, distinguish in its treatment between what I will call Croatian and Serb, military or non-military?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. During the most difficult days when Vukovar was occupied, it didn't matter which ethnic group someone belonged to, which religious affiliation or whatever. The same medical treatment, the same medical assistance, was given to all, regardless of all these different features that I've enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the hospital building itself, the structure. How much floors did the hospital have, let us say, in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In August 1991, the hospital had the following components: The basement, comprising an atomic shelter; the ground floor, with the internal diseases ward; first floor, with gynaecology and maternity ward; the second floor with surgery; and a third floor was added that was never finished, but it was roofed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with the second floor of the -- the floor that you say dealt with surgery. Were you able to use that floor throughout August and afterwards for operations?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, the hospital was shelled for the first time. Those of us who were not familiar with the types of weapons learned that this was a mortar fire which broke window panes and inflicted damage on the ceilings in operating room. Therefore, we had to move the operating room a floor below, to the gynaecology ward. Since the windows and ceilings and certain patient rooms were damaged as well, we moved the patients from those rooms to the basement. That was the first time we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we are dealing with August - and obviously it's difficult to just classify August specifically - but to give an indication at that time when you removed the surgical wards down to the basement area, are you able to assess the percentage of casualties in respect of civilian and non-civilian?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Initially there was a large percentage of civilians, between 60 and 75 per cent. The rest were members of the ZNG and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As time went on - and we'll say September, October, November - can you give an indication to the Court of the number of individuals who were being admitted to the hospital with injuries?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: As time went by, the fall came and the daily intensity of shelling increased. The entire city of Vukovar was shelled as was the hospital. The number of newly admitted persons and persons with grave injuries increased. Initially there were 40 to 50 admitted persons a day, and by October the number grew to between 70 and 80 persons who were wounded and came to the hospital daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about the geographic location of the hospital itself. Knowing the hospital and presumably the area around the hospital, what I will call hinterland, can you tell the Court where the nearest obvious military target would have been or military building would have been?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the hospital itself there was not a single military building except for what existed at the distance of 150 to 200 metres, and that was the police administrative building. This was a police building. As for military installations or buildings, there were none in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, if we're talking about August/September, would you be able to estimate just for those two months how many times the hospital was hit with fire that was not rifle fire?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I believe that hospital was never hit by rifle bullets. I think that it was exclusively hit by shells and plane bombs as well as mortar shells, multi-barrelled rocket launchers, Howitzer guns, and all types of weapons except for rifles. All of those missiles were fired at the hospital. Sometimes on a daily basis, at least that's the information I received from the wounded with whom I shared the same fate, I heard from them that daily up to 100 shells landed on the hospital and nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did that apply to October and November as well?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: From October it was incessant up until 17th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you can understand, either personally or from others, was there any method adopted to try and distinguish a building, a hospital building, to protect it from or perhaps to identify it as being a hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the hospital a huge, white sheet was placed with the red cross on it. It almost touched the hospital. It was visible from the air and perhaps even from other elevations. Another one was placed on the hospital itself. It is possible that there were some other markings, but I'm positive about these two. These markings of the International Red Cross, as I said, were visibly displayed. Throughout that incessant, continuous shelling, we were convinced that they were targeting the hospital on purpose because they used the markings as a guide to guide their missiles and to ensure that they targeted it in an easier way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the atomic shelter at Borovo Komerc. Was that particular atomic shelter used by the hospital in any way?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The shelter at Borovo Komerc was also housed in the basement area. The hospital used this shelter in order to relieve the pressure on the hospital itself. It was impossible for the hospital to keep all the wounded and sick; and therefore, after recovering those wounded who did not require constant surgical or medical attention were moved to Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long or up until what time did you send recovering patients to Borovo Komerc? Can you give the Court an indication of what month that was.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That was up until the 10th, or rather, the 6th of November, 1991. After that, it was impossible because Borovo was cut off from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how far away was Borovo from Vukovar itself, Vukovar Hospital as a reference point?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Roughly between three and four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You used the phrase "relieved pressure on the hospital." When you were actually sending patients to Borovo Komerc, how many patients did you actually have in the Vukovar Hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In those days, as I have told you, every day in October we received between 70 and 80 [as interpreted] wounded persons, and occasionally, although not very often, some persons who were very sick; the hospital was just more than full. There was no room in the corridors, in the rooms, in the atomic shelter. Wherever it was possible and at least safe to some degree, safe from the shells, we used that space. Occasionally we even put two patients in the same bed because we had so many of them. Sometimes we even had to put them under beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We know that on the 19th of October [Realtime transcript read in error "November] that Medecins Sans Frontieres evacuated over a hundred people or patients from the hospital. Do you remember that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The patients that were taken away by Medecins Sans Frontieres, can you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Wrong month, Mr. Lukic? Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something else. On page 25, line 3, the witness said that there were about 500 patients, and this is not recorded in the transcript. So I just wanted to draw your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the correct month, Mr. Moore. I think November is shown in the transcript for the evacuation of Medecins Sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it was October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again so that there's a continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, just to repeat the question to assist you. The 19th of October we know there was an evacuation of patients by Medecins Sans Frontieres. What type of patient was evacuated on that occasion, please?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I think that some 107 or 112 patients were evacuated by Medecins Sans Frontieres; they were taken by them from the Vukovar Hospital. These were seriously injured patients. We, physicians, selected them based on our assessment that they were those who were extremely endangered and could no longer continue staying in the Vukovar Hospital because of the conditions that prevailed there. We believed that they needed to be evacuated in order to recover more speedy and under better conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, about that evacuation and the medical care that was taken of the seriously injured patients. Are you able to assist the Court in telling them about the level of care that was adopted on the 19th of October evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I can tell you how the patients were taken out and boarded on to vehicles that were supposed to drive them along the pre-agreed road. This was pre-agreed by General Raseta in Zagreb during the negotiations conducted in the Hotel E in Zagreb. These negotiations were conducted between General Raseta, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and the Croatian government. In order to speed up transportation and ensure urgent medical attention, they were supposed to take the following route: Vukovar, Bogdanovci, Marinovci, Nustar, Vinkovci, and then further on they were supposed to be hospitalised. We at the hospital had constant contact with Zagreb. We inquired about whether they had arrived. However, we learned that it wasn't until after some 16 or 17 hours of arduous travelling on field roads through dirt that they were handed over to the Croatian medical representatives. These people were in a very serious condition, exhausted. Two patients died en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What steps -- as far as you can recollect, what steps were taken to ensure what I would call continuing medical care on the route from Vukovar to Zagreb? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I do. Some of the care was provided by Medecins Sans Frontieres with the accompanying medical personnel. There were also nurses who were from the Vukovar Hospital. After they crossed the bridge in Luzac, which is a suburb of Vukovar, the convoy was taken over by the Yugoslav People's Army. From then on the convoy travelled under their supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we deal then, please, with the 18th of November. Other topics have perhaps been covered by witnesses and I may return to them generally. But I would like to deal, please, with the actual surrender of Vukovar on or around the 18th of November. Just addressing that date, do you remember any Red Cross personnel coming to the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. But not to the hospital itself, rather in front of the hospital. On the 18th, which was a Monday, the 18th of November, 1991, some time in the early afternoon hours two personnel carriers of the JNA arrived. They pointed their barrels towards the hospital. A captain came out of one of the personnel carriers, a captain of the JNA. Dr. Bosanac, myself, and Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili, stood in front of the entrance because there was an agreement reached between the International Red Cross, General Raseta, and Croatian government that the International Red Cross would take over the hospital, the wounded, sick, and medical staff and take them to the free territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember at what time those personnel carriers came, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In the early afternoon hours, perhaps at around 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And this captain, was he the only officer, JNA officer, that you saw that afternoon or day?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. Following that, near the hospital as we were still standing there awaiting for the representative of the International Red Cross we saw - now I'm giving you my personal account - Major Sljivancanin, Nicholas Borsinger who were arguing about not something. I heard the following words uttered. Major Sljivancanin said: Sir - he was addressing Borsinger - I am in charge here. This is the country where my orders are followed, and it will be as I say. If you find it objectionable, please go back to where you had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what Borsinger said to Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I can only speculate, but I didn't hear, therefore I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You used the word "arguing." Can you describe to the Court what it was you actually saw that you came to the conclusion it was an argument?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: We received information from Zagreb that an agreement had been signed, stipulating that we would be taken over by the representatives of the International Red Cross. Based on that, I understood in that argument that Mr. Borsinger insisted on abiding by the agreement that had been signed by General Raseta, as the JNA representative, International Red Cross, and Croatian government. Represented by the health minister, Professor Andrija Hebrang.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... seems a perfectly obvious question. I can't give you the evidence. How did you know it was an argument as opposed to a normal, rational discussion?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: One could tell, both based on their face expression and gestures. I think it is very easy to tell apart a pleasant conversation or just a normal conversation from a conversation which seems pretty tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you -- were you able to assess the manner and attitude of Sljivancanin to the Red Cross representative?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I concluded that Sljivancanin was quite arrogant, acted victorious, seemed overconfident, and that that was his attitude towards the representative of the International Red Cross. I concluded this based on his firm tone of voice and very stern gestures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about a captain arriving. Did that captain actually speak to you at all that day?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No, no. The captain entered the hospital followed by a unit of the JNA. They placed guards with weapons in front of all large openings in the hospital. There were too many of them due to destruction inflicted by shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to continue asking questions about the 18th, but I just want to follow this captain for a moment, evidentially follow. Was that the only time that you met that captain?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That was the first time, but I'm greatly saddened to say that I met him again both on the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with your meeting with this captain on the 19th. Did you ever discover this captain's name?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the morning of the 19th, it might have been around 8.00 or 9.00, I can't say, the same captain from last night appeared, accompanied by a soldier. He came up to me and he said, Doctor, my name is Captain Radic. From now on -- or as of now, consider yourself under arrest. You must not leave this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you any doubt at all that the captain that you saw on the morning of the 19th was the same captain that you saw the previous day, on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then return to the 18th, the evidence that you were giving was that the captain entered -- Captain Radic, entered followed by a unit of JNA. The JNA soldiers themselves, how long did they remain at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The soldiers remained until 5.00 p.m., when it began to grow dark. After that, the soldiers left only to be replaced by paramilitary Chetnik soldiers or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say who were the military leaders of those Chetnik soldiers who replaced the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I didn't know who their leaders were, nor do I know now who their leaders were at the time. I do know, however, who appeared with them and appeared to lead them, a man named Bogdan Kuzmic, who had been an employee of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The man Bogdan Kuzmic, if we deal with the evening of the 18th, what was he doing that evening?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That evening Bogdan Kuzmic and the captain inspected the hospital, or rather, inspected the basement in which the wounded, sick, medical staff, and all those who sought refuge in the hospital were. They had arrived from basements all over Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm afraid I have to interrupt because we're running to the end of tape. We need to have our first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume then at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just recap, please, the evidence that you gave before the adjournment. You said that that evening, the evening of the 18th, Bogdan Kuzmic and the captain that we know as Captain Radic inspected the hospital or inspected the basement where the wounded, sick, and medical staff were. When you use the phrase "inspected" what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: My intention was to say that they visited all the rooms where the wounded, ill, and medical staff were as well as citizens who had arrived from other basements. The objective of this visit was to identify some of the wounded and civilians who would later, on the 20th, be taken from the hospital and who were eventually to end up at Ovcara. And the other thing, the next day, the 19th of November, the rest of them were taken away. Certain individual medical workers and drivers were taken away. And nothing has been heard of them to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to focus on the evening of the 18th and the morning of the 19th of November. Now, at that time are you able to assess or were you able to assess how many wounded persons were in the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: At that time, on the evening on the 18th, there were over 450 wounded at the hospital. In addition to those, there were a number of sick persons who had no firearm injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I deal with the group of patients generally, are you able to say if any of those patients left the hospital on the evening of the 18th, morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: To my knowledge, on the evening of the 18th and morning of the 19th, none of the wounded left the hospital or the -- any of the other patients for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about Bogdan Kuzmic. You have told us that he was with Captain Radic that evening. Who was Bogdan Kuzmic? How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Bogdan Kuzmic had worked for several years at the hospital's reception, the reception of the Vukovar Hospital. He knew the hospital staff, and he was familiar with the layout of the hospital. He was not a particularly educated person. I believe he had only completed his primary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say what his political affiliation was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I must admit that I was not aware of his political affiliation, of Bogdan Kuzmic's political affiliation, until he showed up at the hospital on the 18th of November as a member of a paramilitary unit, or rather, a reservist, a JNA reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know of a man called Marko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the 18th, 19th of November, do you know where he was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, Marko Mandic -- in the morning during the last operation at the Vukovar Hospital Marko Mandic had still been assisting me in treating a girl who had been hit by shrapnel. Her name was Sanja Vidic. She was three years old, and she had sustained a serious injury to her upper leg and stomach. He was a very good plaster technician, so he applied a plaster cast to her upper leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if he remained in the hospital or whether he left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. On the morning of the 19th of November, Bogdan Kuzmic came to the hospital. And on the morning of the 19th, a JNA captain also appeared who told me his last name was Radic. After that, Marko Mandic disappeared from the Vukovar Hospital as well as some other ambulance drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the behaviour of the -- what you have described, the paramilitary soldiers who replaced the JNA on the evening of the 18th. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did the -- can you tell the Court if the behaviour towards patients changed throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. On the evening of the 18th after, as I have said, Bogdan Kuzmic and the JNA captain -- rather, after they arrived in the hospital and inspected all the basement rooms in which the wounded and sick were, after they left and when I managed to go and see some of those wounded and sick people, they told me that they had been physically and mentally abused and that they were afraid for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did they say what way -- when you say the phrase "physically abused," did the patients describe what was being done to them? And from now on, please, can we refer to the captain as Captain Radic so we know exactly who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: They told me that in each of the rooms they entered they called them Ustashas, they called them slaughterers. They told them that they would meet the very same end and that they knew full well who had been doing what in Vukovar, cursing them all the time. They tried to touch those parts of their bodies, which on account of their injuries were hurting the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As a surgeon, can you just explain the significance of wounds that have been caused by shrapnel or artillery fire, the nature of the injury, please.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: There is a significant difference between wounds caused by a rifle bullet or those caused by shrapnel, no matter if they were caused by bombs dropped by planes or shells fired by mortars, guns, or rather, artillery weapons. There is a third difference, too. Phosphorous bombs were also dropped on Vukovar. These have a particularly horrific effect on those hit, or rather, on those whose bodies are affected by burning phosphorous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How exposed is a wound usually if it is a direct consequence of shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: When is person is hit by shrapnel, there is seldom just one wound. There's usually a lot of shrapnel, and shrapnel being of irregular shape it tends to bring into the wound, so to speak, all of the surrounding material that the wounded person may happen to wear at the time, some of the dust present in the environment, pieces of wood, pieces of dirt. Shrapnel propels these bits of matter, as it were, at great speed so that these bits of wood and even bones shattered by shrapnel become, as it were, secondary or additional shrapnel or shards that may prove to cause even greater damage to the tissue. A gun-shot wound has a point of entry. It drills a channel through the flesh, as it were. This depends on whether we are talking about a dumb-dumb bullet or just a regular, standard issue bullet. This depends on the calibre of the rifle that was used to fire the bullet. As I said, there is an entry, there is a channel through which the bullet passes, and there is usually an exit. And the exit channel and entry all depend on these factors that I have enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that the patients had said that Radic and Kuzmic had tried to touch those parts of their bodies that had been injured. Are you, as a surgeon, able to assess the level of pain --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. This was not the first occasion, but I didn't react earlier. Later on I will explain to you, when the time comes, the character of this evidence. The Prosecutor keeps putting words into the witness's mouth, and now he has gone too far. He never put questions about Captain Radic, linking him to any wounds and so on. Later on we will try to establish whether this was Captain Radic at all or not. But I would like to ask my colleague from the Prosecution not to put any more leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, I did clarify the identification of the captain on the 19th. I brought it back to the 18th. The witness referred specifically to "the captain" and "Kuzmic" going into the hospital. I will locate, if I can, the part of evidence that was given in relation to it. Would Your Honour forgive me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say, Mr. Moore, while you're looking, my note and recollection is that the witness said after the two people, one of who he named as Captain Radic had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And there is nothing to -- and he spoke of the paramilitaries doing these things. I don't think there is any link in the evidence between these threats to patients and the physical handling of them and the two people who did an inspection with the doctor. If there is such a link, I don't believe it has yet emerged in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate, but certainly Your Honour's recollection is correct that there was reference to Kuzmic and Radic going to inspect. The doctor then said that he spoke to the patients after they had left and they complained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My note --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- that they had been physically and mentally abused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- is of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can clarify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- with the witness. That's probably the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the point is - I think that is the core of Mr. Borovic's objection - you're making a positive connection that isn't presently established by the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just look at the transcript for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just read out what I have located on the transcript. At 34 -- it really starts at 5. The question: "Can you tell the Court if the behaviour towards the patients changed throughout this period? "A. Yes. On the evening of the 18th, after, as I've said, Kuzmic and the JNA captain, rather, after they arrived in the hospital and inspected all the basement rooms in which the wounded and sick were, after they left, when I managed to go and see some of those wounded and sick people, they told me they had been physically and mentally abused and they were afraid for their lives. "Q. Did they say what way? When you say the phrase 'physically abused,' did the patients describe what had been done to them? And from now on, please, can we refer to the captain as Captain Radic. "A. They told me that in each of the rooms they entered, they called them Ustashas. They called them slaughterers. They told them that they would meet the very same end, and they knew full well who had been doing what in Vukovar, cursing them all the time. They tried to touch those parts of their bodies, which on account of their injuries were hurting the most." There's no reference at all to TOs. The "they" by logical construction refers to both Radic and Kuzmic. There is no reference at all to the TOs or paramilitaries inflicting this. The logical inference, in my submission, is the two gentlemen who went in, Radic and Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Moore, that instead of logical inferences you might find what is the actual evidence of the witness about this, whether there were only these two people who had inspected the basement and so on. But at the moment, I would suggest that Mr. Borovic is well entitled to object to your positive assertion on the basis of that evidence, that that is the effect of the present evidence. So it's just a matter of clarification. Now, is there something more, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In order to clarify this issue whether the witness said that this involved two persons, one of whom was Captain Radic and the other Mr. Kuzmic, or that he referred to representatives of paramilitary organisations, I would simply like to say that on page 33 or 34, line 24, reflects a question put by Mr. Moore: "I'd like to deal with the behaviour of what you described as paramilitary soldiers who replaced the JNA on the evening of the 18th. Do you follow?" Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. But I think that will indicate to you, Mr. Moore, if it hadn't been to this moment why I have understood this evidence to be referring to conduct of paramilitaries. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to clarify, and I hope in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be wonderful, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you have described to us complaints made to you about abuse of patients. Did the patients say who it was who was abusing them and hurting them?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, they did say that. Since most of them, or at least some of them, knew Bogdan Kuzmic, they mentioned him; the captain accompanied him. I must say that they didn't say so often that he was the one insulting them and cursing them, but he did inflict pain on the wounded. What they told me is that they were the precursors of the mistreatment that was to follow. Later on during the night, certain members of paramilitary formations entered their rooms, as did even JNA soldiers. They also continued mistreating them in both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I then deal, please, with the next occasion that you saw or met Captain Radic. For sequence, would you be kind enough, please, to tell us when it was and, again, what he said to you on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, 1991, at around 9.00 or 10.00, at any rate before noon, as I have said a JNA captain showed up. He introduced himself to me then as Captain Radic. He told me that pursuant to the orders of his superior, he would shut me in a room from which I was not allowed to go out. On that occasion, he also took a medical technician, Ante Aric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that room for?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: There was a guard in front of the room, and I remained in that room until evening, until about 7.00, when the guard moved away. I then went to see the wounded and sick. And as it was impossible to provide any further medical assistance, I tried to calm the wounded and sick and give them some hope, although they had become hopeless after all the mistreatment. They lost any hope that they would survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the situation before we move on, the situation in relation to Captain Radic introducing himself. Here we have a situation where you are aware that allegations are being made that the wounded are being mistreated. Did you ever tell Captain Radic that there had been complaints by the patients about mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission on page 40, line 4, I saw that my learned friend from the Prosecution is directly placing words in the witness's mouth; therefore, I object to this line of questioning. This is a typical example of leading questions being put to the witness. This was just one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I submit that is not a leading question. Evidence has being given in relation to a scenario where there has been evidence in respect of complaints made to the doctor. I am perfectly entitled to ask or to direct the doctor's attention to the issue before the Court and to ask whether in actual fact those complaints were ever communicated to -- those complaints were ever directed to captain -- whether he directed those complaints to Captain Radic. That is not a leading question. It is an option -- or the witness has an option either to say yes or no. A leading question specifically directs the witness to one particular answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. On this occasion, I agree with what you have put, Mr. Moore. The question is in two parts. The first is directing attention to a particular part of the previous evidence, and the second is asking directly whether that has been passed on to Captain Radic. I don't see in that a leading question, Mrs. Tapuskovic. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I talked to them, or rather I asked Captain Radic because he told me that he had studied together with a doctor -- that as a student he knew a doctor who used to work in the Vukovar Hospital. Therefore, later on I asked him whether he knew why the wounded in the Vukovar Hospital had been mistreated the previous night and why they had been tortured. He replied that it was pursuant to the orders or upon permission of the commander, Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You -- do carry on, sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: And then in passing he said to Ante Aric that, It would be good if you changed some of the clothing you have on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just stop you for a moment. Clearly you've told us about being placed in a room, and I asked you about whether you asked Captain Radic a question or not. Let us move on in time to when you were in the room with Aric. Now, did Aric ever leave that room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Aric did leave the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In the morning at around 10.00, or perhaps 11.00, I think it was about 10.00, accompanied by Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was there any conversation in your hearing between Radic and Aric?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No, except for what I said about Captain Aric saying to Ante Aric that he had to change some of his clothing -- or rather, that it would be a good idea if he changed some of the clothing and footwear he had on him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of footwear did Aric have on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Aric had some type of boots on his feet. As for his clothing, under a white coat, because he was a medical technician and he wore one, he had a T-shirt which was similar to a camouflage T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long was Aric away for? Are you able to help us on that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Aric was absent for almost 24 hours. He appeared on the following day sometime around noon or 2.00 p.m., once again accompanied by Captain Radic, who had taken him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak to Aric about what had happened to him in that 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Aric told me that he was taken to a room, where they put him on a chair, where they tied him. Then they pulled his head back, opened his mouth, and poured a bottle of wine in so that he was almost completely out. Prior to that, they questioned him. And as they were not pleased with his answers, they acted in the manner described by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he say who was present at this incident?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. He said that Major Sljivancanin was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did he indicate what sort of questions were being asked of him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: He asked him why he had come from Zagreb to Vukovar, what was the reason for that, whether he brought in weapons, whether he used weapons, where he hid weapons, whom he had killed, who issued orders to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know where Aric actually came from? Was he a local of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Mr. Ante Aric was a medical technician born in Slavonia, born and grew up and lived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would now like to move on in time, if I may, to the evening of the 19th, morning of the 20th of November. Did you remain in the small room that you had been placed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: In the evening of the 19th of November. As I have said, at around 1900 hours he -- or rather, the guard who stood in front of the room where I was shut disappeared. Therefore, I was able to go out and visit the wounded, sick, and others. I also went to see my wife, because on the 17th of November a large number of residents of Vukovar came to the hospital, fearing for their lives, seeking salvation at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went out and you met your wife, if we move on to the morning of the 20th, did you have any contact with any officers of the JNA or other military personnel?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No, not until the morning. However, in the morning, on the 20th of November, at around 8.00, once again Major Sljivancanin appeared at the hospital and ordered all medical staff to assemble in a room that was used to put plaster on patients' extremities whenever needed. Almost entire medical staff, almost all of us, did assemble there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was Sljivancanin alone at that time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin then entered the room on his own, although he had been escorted as far as the room by someone who I believed had the rank of lieutenant colonel, a man by the last name of Ivezic who was a surgeon. I didn't know his first name. He was working as a surgeon in Novi Sad. He did not come into the plaster room, but rather Major Sljivancanin did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When Major Sljivancanin came into the room, can you remember what he said to the assembled people?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. The words are impossible to forget. When he started speaking first he said, I am Major Veselin Sljivancanin, a major of the Yugoslav People's Army. I am the one giving orders here. Everything is under my command. Do not be confused by all these people in military uniforms, different military uniforms with different insignia. These are young people, and nowadays young people like to dress in all sorts of ways and wear all sorts of different insignia. This speech lasted for about -- well, up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you any idea approximately what time Sljivancanin made that speech? Please don't guess if you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: He made that speech - and this is something that I'll never forget - on the 20th of November, 1991, at about 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What happened to you after Sljivancanin had made this address to the people?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Once Sljivancanin had addressed the people, I was again placed in detention. However, in the corridor outside the plaster room I saw a number of nurses and other non-medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time speak to the gentleman that you called Ivezic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. That day, that morning, following Major Sljivancanin's speech in the plaster room, some of the staff who had not attended the meeting told me that a major number of wounded were taken to a special exit from the hospital. I asked Ivezic, counting on some degree of solidarity between doctors, what had become of the wounded and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did he reply to that question?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. He said, Colleague - because that's how he addressed me - everything here is happening according to orders Major Sljivancanin. For this reason, I'm unable to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know of anybody else from the hospital spoke to Ivezic in respect of the missing individuals?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Right there and then I saw Marica Mokos, a nurse who was crying, addressing Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Ivezic asking him to bring back her husband as well as some other persons who had also been led away to the buses on which there were already some wounded. Lieutenant colonel replied, For that I need to go and speak to Major Ivezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That can't be right. I think that may be an error.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I need to go and speak to Major Sljivancanin. I'm sorry. I need to go and ask him for permission so that I would be able to bring your husband back from the bus and to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that person who spoke to Ivezic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Marica -- Nurse Marica Mokos, M-o-k-o-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you at any time personally aware of people having been removed from the hospital that morning?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: At this time I was personally aware because, as I have said already, I had been told by those who were not in the plaster room. These help workers told me that a large number of wounded had been taken away and hoarded onto buses. This occurred on the side of the hospital where the exit is facing the road that crosses the entire town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just -- I may come back to that topic in a moment, but did you at any time see either a monitor or a Red Cross representative on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th, I did not see any representatives of the International Red Cross. It wasn't before 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, please, to look at a diagram that you have drawn and that has been tendered as -- will be tendered, I hope, as an exhibit. It's ERN number 04643050. So there's no mystery about this, to assist the Court, in what will be called reproofing, the witness drew this map and the Court should have a copy of it. Can that be shown on the screen? If it can't, we have hard copies. You'll forgive me a moment while I just locate my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate the hard copies, Mr. Moore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think there are three copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, we're now in the electronically, revolutionary stage. I'm going to see if we can use the magic pencil to point out one or two parts of this map. And if I'm wrong, forgive me, it's your evidence, not mine. Let us just confirm that this is a map that you drew, I think, two days ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is entirely of your making without assistance?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In general terms what does it show?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: It shows the basement of the Vukovar Hospital, the way it was during the attack and aggression against Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
