utterances.text: The way I try and deal - note the word try and deal - with maps and diagrams is I imagine it as a clock with the figures 12 around to 3 on the right, 6 at the bottom, and 9 on the left. Now, if we look at what I would call 12.00, there appears to be parallel lines inside a box. What is that, please? What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: If we are looking at 12.00, then this is the main entrance to the Vukovar Hospital, and then down to the basement. But this supplied to those patients where no urgent intervention was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you the questions; if you can just keep your answers fairly short and we'll try and locate where is where. So can you just put just a dot, please, where you say the main entrance is. Use the pen to touch the electronic screen. Well, I haven't seen anything as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does the Court have any indication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, would you be kind enough just to mark that as number 1.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please point out the other main exits or entrances for that hospital, doing it systematically, one at a time, telling us what is what.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I'm using a number 2 to mark it. This is the main entrance that was always used to enter the hospital for urgent cases as well as regular ones, and it was also used by visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just listen to the question, please. The building itself, does it have -- you mentioned the plaster room. Where is the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I will use a number 3 to mark the plaster room, which was in the basement next to the surgical clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's number 3 on the diagram. Can we see close to that number any exit or entrance for the basement?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm using a number 4 to mark the emergency admission and emergency surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have just made a mark after number 4 where there seems to be arrows. What exactly is that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The arrows show the spot where an ambulance could approach the building to bring the wounded to the emergency ward as well as the emergency entrance to the basement and to the surgery clinics to the left and right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we look at what I will call 5.00, there appears to be a bent arrow above the date of the 9th of the 11th. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. This is number 5. This is the so-called gynaecology entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, would you be kind enough, then, please, to show us with an X where it was Major Sljivancanin had his meeting.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Please pay close attention to number 3. I will use the number X to mark that room. This is the room where Major Sljivancanin made a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough, using the figure Y, to indicate where your small room was that you were kept in.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I'm pointing at the small room in which I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the individuals who had been removed, are you able to show on the diagram with Z where it was they had been located before their removal?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: By your leave, I will show you where the wounded were. Next I will show you how they were led away. This is number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I would like to do, please, is to do it one at a time. Where were the individuals located before they were removed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Before they were removed they were located next to this letter Y. Next to it there's a waiting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you draw, please, on the electronic board the place where the wounded people had been kept before being removed.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you have drawn dots. Can you perhaps do it in something that's slightly more obvious.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it a case they were in small groups or this denotes, what I will call, a general area?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: These circles comprised the entire area that's been marked. It was filled to bursting point, as it were. There was no room to fit a needle or, indeed, to pass between all the wounded and ill. There was simply too many people in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the first part. May we deal with the second. You said that -- how they were removed. Can you show, please, on the diagram how it was and where they were removed to.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The wounded where you can see the circles. Wounded were removed from each of these circles, and exit number 5 was used to take them out of the hospital and herd them on to buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say "exit 5," is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an intervention. I'm talking about page 51, line 8. The witness said that a number of wounded were removed from each of the circles, and if he can please confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with the utmost respect, I thought the witness had indicated -- he had drawn circles and then had gone on to say you couldn't put a needle between them. I thought I'd actually clarified the issue of whether this was small bundles of people or whether it was a larger group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has no doubt that many wounded were removed from each of the areas marked by circles. If that helps you, Mr. Lukic, that is the effect of the language that's used by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll clarify then if --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you may not be an artist. You have drawn small circles on your map. Does this indicate that there are small groups of people at these locations or does it indicate that there was the whole area covered? Can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The whole area that I have encircled or where I placed circles was filled with wounded people. But as you can see, there were a number of petitions in certain places and that's why I used small circles to mark these spots, just in order to show that all these rooms were brimming with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you used the word "brimming with the wounded." When you came out of the meeting, was the area still brimming with the wound?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I apologise. When I left the meeting at number 3 and passed the area between number 3 and the letter Y, I met Lieutenant Colonel Ivezic and Nurse Marica Mokos. I learned that a large group of wounded had been taken away by entrance -- exit number 5. I knew that in these rooms that I have marked there were a lot less wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we then move on, please. You say that they were taken out of exit 5. If we look at the diagram itself, what is to the right of the diagram? Can you describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On the right side of this sketch there is an exit from the hospital. In front of the exit there is an area where buses had been parked in which the wounded were placed or, better said, herded, those who had been taken from the basement through the gynaecology entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, I'd ask you, from the actual Vukovar Hospital to the bridges over the Vuka River, are you able to assess what the distance would be?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: From the hospital to the bridges there is a distance of some 400 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I at this time have no further questions in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, first did you want number 6 to be marked, that external exit and buses? Or is that off the plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I better ask the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 6, can we see number 6 where the road is that runs to the Vuka River? Would you be kind enough to mark it for us.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The number 6 here depicts six buses into which they herded the wounded. I will indicate with dots the exit used by the buses to leave the compound as they headed towards the Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the dots that seemed to go to the north, or to 12.00, is that the direction of the Vuka?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. The direction of the Vuka and the bridges over that river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender this plan, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm anxious that we don't lose it, given that there's a time. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court are considering having a short break. If the Court is considering that, this might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is going to be a convenient moment, Mr. Moore. We've hung on trying to ensure that we could finish with this plan and get it tendered before it was electronically lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the plan is being saved and it will be Exhibit Number 64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that perhaps it would be prudent also to put the original document in unmarked as an exhibit. I don't know if my learned friends would agree with that course. I thought it would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 65, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that you had not seen any monitors or Red Cross representatives on the 20th, my recollection is until about 2.00, but I may be in error on that. When did you actually first come across the Red Cross/monitors?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The first time I saw the Red Cross representative was on the 18th, as I have said, in front of the hospital when he talked to Major Sljivancanin, that is, Nicholas Borsinger. The other meeting with a representative of the International Red Cross was on the 20th at around 1400 hours. A representative of the International Red Cross came to the hospital, to the basement. He approached me and talked to me. He asked me whether I knew how many patients there were and what had happened to cause the situation where there were very few medical staff members, wounded, and patients in the hospital. This representative of the Red Cross was a young person, shortish. In my view, this representative of the International Red Cross was an Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak any Italian at that time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I can understand Italian. I have some passive knowledge of the language, and I think that that was quite sufficient for us to be able to communicate and to explain what had happened in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, what was the topic of discussion with the International Red Cross representative?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The conversation with the representative of the International Red Cross was as follows. What is the treatment that the wounded receive? Were Geneva Conventions complied with? And would I make a list of the remaining wounded still in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you make a list of the remaining people at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Following the conversation with the International Red Cross, an anaesthesiologist from the military medical academy in Belgrade came with me. He went alongside and checked whether I put on the list all of the wounded remaining in the hospital. I made the list in two copies, one of which was taken over by the representative of the International Red Cross and the other one by the anaesthesiologist from the military medical economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What happened to you that day after your discussion with the representative of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: On that day after the list was made up, the one received both by the representative of the International Red Cross and the military representative, because that's who the anaesthesiologist from the military medical academy was. He also had a rank. So after they took the lists, it was getting closer to twilight - it was close to 5.00 - Captain Radic came to the hospital and an officer, a lady officer. I believe that she was a major of some 40, 45 years. Upon entering the hospital, they took me out of the room that I've pointed out to the Trial Chamber. This lady officer came up to me and asked me why I had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When this occurred, where was the Red Cross representative?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: The International Red Cross representative was present; he watched this. Once he saw me being led away into a military vehicle which was parked in the area in front of the emergency admission, the one you could see on the sketch, he protested about them once again violating international conventions which applied to the hospitals and medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of his protest?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: They denied the protest. They told him that it was none of his concern. This involvement of the International Red Cross representative angered the lady officer, and she ordered the soldier who had been guarding me up at that time to take me to a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we can deal with this in a shortened form. Where were you actually taken to?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: As I was ordered to enter a military vehicle, Ante Aric came with Captain Radic. Ante Aric, pursuant to an order, was also put on the military vehicle. After that, the lady officer came into the vehicle. She sat next to the driver. Behind them were the soldier and Captain Radic. We were then taken to the barracks, which was located in Vukovar in an area known as Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you any idea of the approximate time that you were taken away in a military vehicle with various parties, including Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: As it was in November, on the 20th of November, I think that this transpired at around 5.00 so that we arrived in the barracks which is not located far away. But due to damaged streets and roads, it took us somewhat longer to reach it, some 15 minutes perhaps. That's how long it took us to get to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have described seeing Captain Radic at 5.00, approximately, that evening. Do you know -- and you have mentioned the International Red Cross representative at approximately 2.00. Did you see Captain Radic between the hours of 2.00 and 5.00 that day?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see him until he escorted Ante Aric and placed him in detention in the same room where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, the same question in relation to Major Sljivancanin. I know about the meeting but I'll still just deal with the timings, 2.00 until 5.00, did you see Major Sljivancanin at all through that period?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. After the meeting in the plaster room in the morning where Major Sljivancanin gave a speech that I've already described to the Trial Chamber, I didn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we deal with the JNA barracks, which are just outside Vukovar itself. How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I remained in the Vukovar barracks for about an hour. They separated Ante Aric there and they brought in Dr. Bosanac. She and I were put in a personnel carrier, military personnel carrier, and taken to the village of Negoslavci. And then via Sidski Banovci, Oriolik, Tovarnik we travelled to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to look at Exhibit 59, which is going to be map 6. I don't know if we've got a hard copy or whether we can do it by electronic form. I would prefer the witness to have a hard copy, please, if there's one available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I pass this to the witness, please. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, this is a map of what I would call the Ovcara hinterland, and I'd like to go on what I would call a voyage of discovery together in respect of some locations. How long had you been in Vukovar prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: At that time I had already been about 25 years in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how good was your knowledge of what I will call the local hinterland?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I think I knew the hinterland well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to look at the map which is on your right. Can you see it? You've actually got a hard copy on your right which is a lot clearer --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you look at the map on your right, it's a hard copy; it's much clearer than this computer representation. Now, we can see that this is Vukovar itself on the Danube. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Using the clock-face again, if we drop immediately south, we can see the village of Negoslavci. Do you see that? I'm sure the usher will help you. It says "Negoslavci."

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much there. There is a reference to the JNA barracks and Velepromet. Do you see that on the map? Can you answer "yes" please.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then if we look at what I will call 4.00 we have got Ovcara. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If one was going to Ovcara by the normal route, by the road, by the road, in 1991 and you were leaving the JNA barracks, can you please point out to us the route on the road, the Tarmac road, that one would normally take. Are you able to do that for us?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991 if one went to Ovcara but taking the asphalt road, then one would go from the Velepromet into the downtown area and then if -- coming from Velepromet, then one would turn right into the street called Stijepana Radica [phoen] and then continue along that road towards Mitnica, which is an area of the town located in the eastern section of Vukovar. Following that, one would take the road leading to Sotin, and prior to reaching Sotin there was a farm and -- a cattle farm called Jakubovac. From then one would turn towards Ovcara, which was known as a cattle farm, or rather, a farm for raising pigs and oxen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if one goes back to the JNA barracks again and we have the road to Negoslavci, which we can see and I've referred you to, are you or were you aware at that time of any other way to get to Ovcara without going through Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Personally, although I often went to Negoslavci as well as the surrounding villages, I never took a different route to Sotin. Therefore, I was not aware of any other way to get to Ovcara aside from the one that I have just indicated. I didn't even know that there was a field road or field path from in front of Negoslavci and on to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you discover that there was what I will call -- or you called a field road from just before Negoslavci to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, I learned about the existence of this road from those who survived the tragic trip to Ovcara. That was the first I learned of the existence of that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you can just put that map away. How long were you kept in custody? You've told us that you were taken to the JNA barracks and Dr. Bosanac was there. Perhaps it's my use of the word "custody." What happened after you had seen Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: While I was alone with the guard in the car the former judge of the Vukovar court was there and asked me about certain judges from Vukovar, if I knew what had become of them or what they had been doing. After that, he left and they brought Dr. Bosanac. We both got in that APC and she told me that they had taken her for an interview with Lieutenant Colonel Mrksic in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal, though, with this day. Here you are at the JNA barracks. Where were you taken after there, please?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: After that, if you look at the sketch, we were close to Velepromet. The JNA barracks was across the way from there. We were taken there. We were taken to Negoslavci in an APC. In Negoslavci, they let us out of the APC, and it was extremely unpleasant because we received verbal threats from people and they were making the slit-throat gesture, meaning we would have our throats slit. However, at this time no one managed to come close to us and we continued, as I said, over Borovik and Sidski Banovci, these are villages on the way, and Tovarnik, this is still in Croatia, until we reached Sid, a town in Serbia, a town in Vojvodina, which is part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to stop for a moment and then I want to quite deliberately take you back to a topic in respect of treatment of patients. It's perfectly clear that there were civilians and wounded, what I would call, military personnel, both JNA and Croatian, in the hospital. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you distinguish between those categories when it came to treatment?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: No. That would have run counter to all ethical principles, to humanitarian law, to the science of medicine. It would also have been against our commitment as human beings to a humanitarian profession such as medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We also know that there was a room specifically for wounded JNA soldiers. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: That is correct. Your Honours, as you know, I said earlier how many wounded people kept coming. At certain points in time, those wounded who were already in the hospital fighting for their lives or merely recovering, because of what they felt at the time would have been likely to harm JNA soldiers or members of paramilitary Chetnik units who were there. This precisely was the reason why they were given the best possible medical attention and assistance and placed in a special room so that they were not subjected to taunts and verbal threats or even physical incidents. This was the reason why there was always a guard standing outside their room providing security for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to have the JNA soldiers placed in a separate room; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. Knowing that there is a lot of unbridled emotion in wartime which unfortunately seems to be the rule not the exception, and given the fact that there were many elderly people and children in Vukovar, people aged between 80 and 90 in old people's homes, as well as children aged six months, there was a need to protect the soldiers from exposure to these emotional states characterised by high stress levels. And that is why Dr. Bosanac and I made a joint decision to have them isolated in a special room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you know a JNA soldier there who was called Sasa Jovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. There were two groups of JNA soldiers. One was Sinisa Miljkovic, the other was Jovic, and the third was Pavle Teofanovic. They were together in the room. Their injuries were serious and life-threatening. Sasa Jovic was an officer, and once he had recovered and realised how we had been treating him at the hospital, him as well as all the other wounded and sick, he requested that he speak to General Raseta. His request was met. He told him, Dear General, these people are saving our lives and yet you are destroying this hospital where lives are being saved. Please protect the hospital because everybody is given the same kind of treatment here and treated alike, regardless of their uniforms or affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember when Jovic -- if we use the 18th of November as a reference point, can you remember when it was Jovic made that telephone call or spoke to Raseta? If you can't, do say so.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically the date, but it must have been at least ten days, more possibly, before the hospital was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know or did you know at that time a gentleman called Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was Dr. Ivankovic, please?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Dr. Mladen Ivankovic is a surgeon. He's a competent surgeon. He came to the Vukovar Hospital later on. Among us ordinary surgeons, so to speak, who were not members of the League of Communists or the Communist Party, we always believed that he had been given a job there by a party decision because he also happened to be the party secretary, a commissioner in the Vukovar Hospital. Soon after, he was given a piece of land in a very favourable spot, unlike many other doctors who had been working in the Vukovar Hospital for a long time significantly contributing to the general health situation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know Tomislav Djuranac?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Dr. Tomislav Djuranac worked in Borovo as a general practitioner. In our medical circles, by the way, he was not held in particularly high regard. The reason was quite simple. He was prone to perhaps have a drop too many on -- more often than not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now move back to you going to Sid on the 20th when you were under what I will call JNA custody. Where did you eventually end up?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Having been brought to Sid, they brought us out of the personnel carrier and took us into a military vehicle made of metal with metal seats, seats inside. And it was night-time. We were taken to Belgrade. In Belgrade they took us to the barracks at Dedina. We stayed there but they didn't just leave us there. Rather, the next morning they drove us back to Sremska Mitrovica, the camp in Sremska Mitrovica, at about 4.00 on the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you just tell us what happened there, please.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: Yes. At Negoslavci Anto Aric was added to the group comprising Dr. Bosanac and myself. The three of us went via Sid, Belgrade, Sremska Mitrovica, and eventually in Sremska Mitrovica as we left the vehicle, they physically abused us and forced us to walk with our heads bowed, hands behind our backs. After we entered a building, Aric and I had our clothes taken away. We were stripped naked. They searched us thoroughly. We remained there for perhaps half an hour naked out in the cold, after which we were allowed to put our clothes back on. They had taken away all of our belongings, everything that there was in our pockets, and they took us to a prison camp, room number 6 on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened at the prison camp? How long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO
utterances.text: I was there for about 17 or 18 days. Every day, or quite often they would take us for interrogations at all times of the day or night. Threats were being made along the way, needless to say. And once we reached the interrogation room I, for one, was questioned by Colonel Stanko. I can't say that he beat me or verbally abused me excessively. However, once he had handed me over to the guards to take me back, physical problems started occurring on my body. After the three of us entered the building where the camp prison was, the three of us, Dr. Bosanac, Ante Aric, and myself, Ante Aric was taken to one side immediately and right there in plain sight - I can't find the right word or a better expression - they thrashed him like a beast. Being a doctor, I wondered if it was possible to beat someone black and blue like that and for that person to still survive. And this happened right there in front of us, I suppose, as a sort of welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, Mr. Moore, is the time when we must adjourn, because the court is now required for another Chamber. Doctor, I'm sorry but we must ask you to return on Monday, when the evidence will continue. We will be sitting next week in the afternoon, starting at 2.15. We will adjourn until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
